documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Emergency departments (EDs) are critical for suicide prevention, yet high workloads often hinder consistent case management. This pilot study assessed the clinical feasibility, usability, and acceptability of CAREBot, a rule-based chatbot designed to support ED-based case management for patients at risk of suicide, among patients and social workers. Methods: We employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Ten patients and three social workers used CAREBot and completed questionnaires assessing usability, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction. Patients’ psychological status was repeatedly assessed using the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R. Semi-structured interviews with social workers explored integration challenges and workflow impacts. Results: Patients rated ease of use (3.9/5) and information clarity (4.4/5) favorably, whereas emotional comfort was rated lower (2.5/5). Over 4 weeks, 191 URL access events were recorded among the 10 patients (mean, 19.1 per patient). Individual PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R score trajectories varied across participants, with both increases and decreases observed. Social workers rated CAREBot favorably for quickly understanding patients’ risk level or condition (4.33/5) and ease of following the scenario flow (5.0/5). Qualitative findings suggested that CAREBot could support initial patient assessments through structured digital screening, although social workers raised concerns regarding risk-scoring accuracy and the management of multiple high-risk patients. Conclusions: CAREBot appears to be feasible and acceptable as an adjunct to ED-based suicide case management, although these preliminary findings require confirmation in larger controlled studies. A rule-based architecture was deliberately selected to provide predictable and controlled interactions in a high-risk environment. Future research should evaluate whether integrating large language models (LLMs) with rule-based safety mechanisms can improve conversational responsiveness and personalization while maintaining patient safety.

documents.abstract: The transition toward a low-carbon hotel sector involves more than the availability of financing or the adoption of technology. It also relates to the ability to transform available resources into usable technical capabilities and organizational commitments that can sustain the implementation of environmental initiatives. Drawing on the sociotechnical systems (STS) perspective, this study examines how financial–structural enabling conditions (FSECs) relate to perceived low-carbon performance (PLCP) through two parallel mechanisms: organizational ethical commitment to sustainability (OESC) and green technological capability (GTC). Using a sample of 587 informants—67 managers and 520 employees—from 103 hotels in Extremadura, Spain, the proposed relationships are analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that more favorable FSECs have a positive direct relationship with perceived low-carbon performance and are also associated with greater development of GTC and OESC. Both mechanisms are positively related to performance, and both proposed indirect pathways receive empirical support. Theoretically, this study extends the sociotechnical perspective on hotel sustainability by positioning FSECs as an enabling context related to environmental performance through distinct but simultaneous organizational and technological mechanisms. Practically, it provides guidance for environmental investment and the design of support programs tailored to hotels’ conditions and needs.

Structural biology mailing lists such as CCP4, CCP-EM, Phenix and COOT contain decades of expert answers to practical problems, but an answer is difficult to find even when it has been given before. A question-and-answer corpus was built from 103,600 messages across the four mailing lists, and threads were classified as questions. The answers were confirmed by the asker’s reply or by the agreement of several participants, identified by three LLM models. This gave 4,320 curated question-and-answer pairs, which were used for fine-tuning and retrieval augmentation for six LLM models, two sizes each from the Mistral, Llama and Qwen families. The LLM models were evaluated under eight conditions: base and fine-tuned, each without retrieval and with retrieval from the software documentation, from the mailing-list corpus, and from both. The base models with mailing-list retrieval were preferred by the LLM judges over the base models alone, the fine-tuned models, and even the base models with retrieval from the software documentation. The data sets and the fine-tuned models are publicly available.

Fire the Neuron is an interactive learning tool designed to reinforce foundational concepts in neuronal physiology through active engagement with immediate feedback. The activity guides students through nine progressive stages exploring the electrical and chemical events involved in neuronal communication. Throughout the activity, students investigate graded potentials, action potential generation, depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization, refractory periods, action potential propagation, and synaptic transmission. Interactive components challenge students to calculate changes in membrane potential, predict whether threshold will be reached, identify the roles of voltage-gated ion channels, and examine the effects of myelination and demyelination on signal propagation. Students also sequence events involved in synaptic transmission and investigate disruptions in neuronal communication. Immediate feedback provides opportunities to evaluate responses, identify misconceptions, and reinforce understanding. The tool is designed primarily for undergraduate anatomy and physiology courses but may also be appropriate for introductory neuroscience and related courses. Instructors can incorporate it into classroom activities, assign it as an independent learning exercise, or recommend it as a supplemental resource for reviewing course material and preparing for examinations. Fire the Neuron is freely accessible through GitHub Pages and can be completed using a standard web browser without downloading additional software or creating an account. The tool was developed with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (AI), with the instructional content, scientific accuracy, and pedagogical design guided and reviewed by the author. The continuous development and integration of public and private Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures require flexible and scalable data access mechanisms that ensure seamless access to IoT data regardless of its source of physical address. Traditionally, retrieving data from different physical sources requires rigid, topology-dependent protocols and high technical skills; this may limit accessibility for a wider range of end-users.Content-Based Addressing (CBA) accesses data based on its attributes or content rather than its network location. Users need an intuitive mechanism to extract IoT values from multiple sources (e.g. public and private sources), removing the need for technical database query knowledge. In a similar way to web search (e.g. Google), users ask questions in natural language based on content, location and time without direct reference to the physical location of the IoT devices that provide the necessary information. This paper proposes a novel, hybrid framework for flexible IoT data access that combines CBA with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based conversational interface. The architecture is built on two core pillars: a Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) layer, coupled with a device registry, that unifies heterogeneous data sources, public APIs and private edge devices, into a single content-addressed store secured by a granular Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism. The second pillar is a Natural Language Query Engine that translates chat-based interrogations into executable system queries.An adaptive imputation service maintains data completeness by detecting missing sensor readings, predicting replacement values, and reconciling predictions when delayed measurements arrive. Together, the framework enables an intuitive experience for IoT data exploration with no technical training needed.

Developing flexible electronics that integrate multimodal sensing, bias-free signal generation, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding is critical for wearable health monitoring, artificial intelligence, and human–computer interaction. Semiconducting Mo2TiC2Tx MXene films show promise for flexible thermoelectrics and EMI shielding, but their relatively low electrical conductivity restricts both the power factor (PF) and the overall EMI shielding effectiveness (SE). Here, we report a van der Waals heterostructure film of Mo2TiC2Tx/TaS2 fabricated via intercalation–exfoliation followed by vacuum-assisted filtration. Heterointerface engineering simultaneously enhances thermoelectric performance and EMI shielding. The electrical conductivity reaches 878.3 S·cm−1 (~23-fold enhancement), and the PF reaches 14.4 μW·m−1·K−2 (~4-fold), while the EMI SE improves from 14.1 to 40.6 dB. The film enables dual-mode sensing free from crosstalk, temperature detection via the Seebeck effect and pressure sensing via piezoresistive response, while maintaining stable signal fidelity under external EMI. Furthermore, the film exhibits photothermoelectric and Joule-heating responses. Integrated with a wireless acquisition module for signal readout and transmission, the sensor enables real-time transmission of temperature and pressure signals. This work provides a strategy for designing flexible heterostructures that synergistically combine bias-free signal generation, multimodal sensing, EMI resilience, and multistimulus responsiveness for next-generation smart electronics.

Tabular foundation models, specifically Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), have revolutionized outlier detection (OD) by enabling unsupervised zero-shot adaptation to new datasets without training. However, despite their predictive power, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, outputting scalar outlier scores that lack the operational context required for safety-critical decision-making. Existing post-hoc explanation methods are often computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment or fail to capture the epistemic uncertainty inherent in zero-shot inference. In this work, we introduce FoMo-X, a modular framework that equips OD foundation models with intrinsic, lightweight diagnostic capabilities. We leverage the insight that the frozen embeddings of a pretrained PFN backbone already encode rich, context-conditioned relational information. FoMo-X attaches auxiliary diagnostic heads to these embeddings, trained offline using the same generative simulator prior as the backbone. This allows us to distill computationally expensive properties, such as Monte Carlo dropout based epistemic uncertainty, into a deterministic, single-pass inference. We instantiate FoMo-X with two novel heads: a Severity Head that discretizes deviations into interpretable risk tiers, and an Uncertainty Head that provides calibrated confidence measures. Extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ADBench) demonstrates that FoMo-X recovers ground-truth diagnostic signals with high fidelity and negligible inference overhead. By bridging the gap between foundation model performance and operational explainability, FoMo-X offers a scalable path toward trustworthy, zero-shot outlier detection.

Abstract and Introduction 1.1 Abstract Conventional AI evaluations overemphasize computational speed and benchmark accuracy, risking a widening gap between expanding compute infrastructure and power demand and social value return. Eliminating deficit compensation via addition and evaluation via negative values, this paper formulates a Human–AI Coexistence model that explicitly separates the Unity Preservation Principle and the Multiplicative Preventive Maintenance Principle. Under the Unity Preservation Principle, unity (1) is set as the societal maintenance baseline, essential factors are evaluated as maintenance ratios F_i(t) \in (0, 1], and contraction relative to unity is captured multiplicatively (F_{\text{society}}(t) = 1 \times \prod_{i=1}^{n} F_i(t)). Under the Multiplicative Preventive Maintenance Principle, the model captures downward trends and decline magnitudes using positive ratios—the preceding-step ratio \Delta_i(t) = \frac{F_i(t)}{F_i(t-1)} and the decline magnitude index D_i(t) = \frac{1}{\Delta_i(t)}—and mitigates downward drift to reduce the likelihood of reaching zero via multiplicative counter-intervention M_i(t) = D_i(t)^{\kappa_i(t)} and F_i(t+1) = \min\big(1,\, F_{\text{base},i}(t+1)\,M_i(t)\big) without additive deficit compensation or negative cause-slope terms. It organizes the framework into a five-layer architecture, a five-stage preventive maintenance process, and 3C³ governance (Consistency, Correspondence, Consensus), supported by verified Steps 0–10 simulations including a no-intervention control comparison, while distinguishing three epistemic tiers and explicit scope limits.

This reflective case study documents how sustained collaboration with ChatGPT helped Jean-Pol Martin make his doctoral dissertation (1985) and habilitation thesis (1994) openly accessible. According to Martin’s retrospective account, AI dialogue introduced publication possibilities he had not previously considered and supported the organization of a process involving digitization, publisher permission, legal assistance and coordination with the University Library of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt. Over approximately two months, at a reported cost of EUR 400, both foundational works were made available through Zenodo and the university’s publication server, KU.edoc. The dissertation’s two microfiche supplements were also digitized and published. Inclusion of the digital editions in the library catalogue was pending at the reporting cut-off. The paper examines the complementary contributions of AI assistance, human initiative and institutional infrastructure. Its contribution to the ongoing exploration of Martin’s human-AI model is a documented implementation process whose outputs extend beyond jointly generated text: publicly accessible primary sources. The study distinguishes demonstrated accessibility from potential future effects on discovery, scholarly reception and citation impact. It also addresses limitations concerning retrospective testimony, machine readability and long-term preservation. Decompression sickness (DCS) is an occupational health problem fundamentally driven by the formation of gas bubbles in the human body, which could be a threat to the life of divers, astronauts and hyperbaric workers. The phenomenon of bubble formation in organisms after decompression provided the earliest experimental evidence for decompression theory. Since then, researchers across different eras have conducted extensive work on biological decompression bubbles, which brought about the establishment of gas nuclei theory. While Yount’s quantitatively calculable Varying Permeability Model (VPM) has been successfully applied to decompression algorithms, its core assumption—the “surface-active skin”—remains experimentally unverified. But recent developments in research on nanobubbles and the Active Hydrophobic Spots (AHS) hypothesis have provided new physicochemical perspectives. This review critically evaluates the theoretical evolution and experimental progress in this field, integrating recent advances in molecular dynamics and interfacial physics. To contribute to shedding light on the unresolved paradox of biological decompression bubbles in vivo, we highlight the significance of the paradigm shift from macroscopic gas dissolution to interfacial mechanics, which may help identify the missing links in current DCS research and outline a new multidisciplinary path forward.

The article examines the development of data-driven research in contemporary social sciences amid the growing use of big data, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. The aim of the study is to analyze publication trends, the thematic structure of this research field, and the prevalence of critical discourse concerning the methodological and epistemological limitations of digital technologies. The empirical dataset comprises 3,779 English-language scientific articles published between 1995 and 2025 and indexed in the Scopus database. The study employs bibliometric analysis, natural language processing (NLP), latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling, bigram analysis, and dictionary-based identification of critical themes. Particular attention is given to data quality, measurement validity, algorithmic bias, and risks associated with generative artificial intelligence. The findings demonstrate substantial growth in publication activity since the 2010s and a shift in thematic emphasis from big data toward machine learning and artificial intelligence. Topic modeling reveals considerable thematic heterogeneity despite the application of similar analytical approaches. Indicators of critical discourse are identified across different thematic areas, although their prevalence remains limited: relevant publications accounted for 9.2% of the annual dataset in 2024 and 9.0% in 2025. The findings indicate that quantitative research expansion is accompanied by thematic fragmentation and a relatively small proportion of publications containing identifiable indicators of critical reflection. The scientific significance of the study lies in systematizing research trends and thematic structures, while its practical significance concerns improving social research methodology and teaching data analysis methods. However, term-frequency analysis cannot directly assess the depth of critical reflection or the degree of theoretical integration within the social sciences. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the findings and drawing broader conclusions. documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about predictive models, but a fluent answer about a model is not necessarily true of it. We propose a framework in which every answer is checked against a reference that independent software computes from the fitted model. The main finding is simple: the LLM was much more accurate when software had done the calculations than when it had to work them out from the model itself. In a confirmatory study with Gemini 2.5 Flash, the LLM correctly answered 16 of 36 questions whose answer follows exactly from the full model description, such as a prediction or a decision path, but 33 of the same 36 once software had computed the values from which the answer follows. A replication with 50 classifiers, five datasets and three LLM configurations, including a reasoning setting and an open-weight model, reproduced this pattern. Without model information, the LLMs declined to answer or guessed at chance level, and verified answers were reported faithfully once their origin was stated. Model-specific calculations should therefore be left to verified software, while the LLM reports and explains the checked results.

documents.abstract: Visible and near-infrared (vis–NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy enable rapid, cost-effective prediction of soil properties. Yet, translating high-dimensional, highly collinear spectra into accurate soil property predictions remains challenging, particularly when employing machine learning. We systematically investigated regression models and dimensionality reduction approaches for spectroscopic modeling across 85 soil property prediction tasks from open benchmark datasets in pedometrics, spanning field-scale digital soil mapping and a global soil spectral library. We compared an in-context learning tabular foundation model (TabPFN), a convolutional neural network (CNN), rule-based regression (Cubist), Random Forest, and partial least squares regression (PLSR) using full spectra as well as features derived from principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares (PLS) latent variables. TabPFN consistently delivered the best overall performance across spectral regions, properties, and scales, including large spectral library tasks with tens of thousands of soil samples. Notably, TabPFN applied directly to full spectra already surpassed all classical baselines, showing that explicit dimensionality reduction is not strictly required for strong performance. Further improvements were achieved through PLS, which proved to be an effective dimensionality reduction strategy for all models. Combining PLS latent variables with TabPFN yielded the best predictions overall, lowering the root mean squared error (RMSE) relative to the strongest classical baseline on 44 of the 46 large-scale spectral library tasks, by a median of 14%. Our findings provide evidence-based guidance for spectroscopic calibration model selection across operational scales, demonstrating that the long-standing advantages of PLSR and modern tabular foundation models complement each other in chemometrics.

Hidden capture is a loss of skill that the people losing it do not notice, combined with a dependence that does not reverse when the pressure behind it eases. The Correction Freeze Problem predicts this pattern, but testing it on human thinking would take decades of data that do not yet exist for generative AI. We therefore built a computer simulation of a population, calibrated to what can be measured today, and followed it across generations in two worlds that share the same machines. In World M, AI mostly replaces people’s own practice, and each generation learns what normal ability looks like from the one before. In World N, AI mostly supports practice, and each generation’s sense of normal ability is anchored in direct experience, including time in nature. The model reproduces today’s rise of AI-written text in student work, the share of people who check AI output, and how loosely people’s opinions of their own thinking track tested performance. The simulations show what a captured world would be like from the inside. Delegation stays modest for a while and then sweeps through most of the population within a few years, because each person who hands over their thinking makes it more normal for everyone else. Skill then drains away without being felt. In World M, the average person’s unaided ability fell to about the bottom tenth of the population before AI, yet people registered only a small part of that loss, about a quarter even a century later, because their machine-assisted work looked as good as ever and everyone around them had declined too. The habit of checking disappeared first: at full delegation, only two people in a hundred still compared the machine’s answers with their own judgment, and when the machine’s error rate was quietly doubled, about one in a hundred noticed within five years. In an illustrative century, easing the pressure after a generation of heavy delegation restored only World N; the other two worlds were still captured half a century later. Staying out of the trap proved far easier than climbing out of it. These findings are conditional projections, not forecasts. Across 2,176 sensitivity runs, the unseen loss appeared every time, and its size depended mainly on two things societies can influence now: whether AI replaces or supports people’s own practice, and whether each generation anchors its sense of competence in direct experience. Whether capture can be undone depended on one quantity not yet measured, how much an individual’s reliance on AI changes from year to year; if reliance churns, capture becomes reversible, though it stays hidden. Several earlier results weakened as the model was corrected, and the main pre-specified test of a final extension came back negative; both are reported.

documents.abstract: Curriculum planning takes time and energy. As concerns about teacher workload and workforce shortages intensify, many education systems are turning to scripted curriculum materials and emerging generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools to support planning, assuming that reducing curriculum work will alleviate teachers’ widely recognised time poverty. Such responses position curriculum planning as a task to be streamlined, standardised, or outsourced. However, they risk oversimplifying the complexity of curriculum work and undervaluing the interpretative processes teachers engage in to meet the diverse needs of their students. Drawing on interviews with eight teachers and curriculum leaders in Australian Capital Territory (ACT) public primary schools, this paper examines how teachers understand curriculum planning and its place within their professional work. Framed through the concepts of interpretative labour and discretionary spaces, the study explores how teachers exercise professional judgement as they adapt, translate, and enact curriculum in response to particular learners and contexts. The findings suggest that teachers may not experience curriculum planning as administrative “busywork”, but as an intellectually demanding, creative, and professionally meaningful aspect of teaching. The findings highlight a tension often overlooked in workload debates: work that demands time and effort is not necessarily work that teachers wish to reduce or remove. Rather, participants described curriculum planning as a key source of professional satisfaction, agency, and connection to students’ learning. We argue that contemporary workload reduction strategies may misrecognise the nature of curriculum work by treating it as an expendable burden rather than a central dimension of professional practice. The paper concludes that addressing teacher workload requires not only reducing unnecessary administrative demands but also recognising and supporting the interpretative labour involved in curriculum making.

Predictive accuracy does not establish that an intervention is effective. This study proposes a decision-centric artificial intelligence workflow combining predictive modelling, SHAP explainability, heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation, policy learning, and intervention-utility evaluation. Four predictive models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) and six causal and uplift estimators (S-Learner, T-Learner, X-Learner, LinearDML, Causal Forest, and Random Forest Two-Model Uplift) were evaluated using a treatment-balanced sample of 500,000 observations from the Criteo benchmark. Binary visit was the primary outcome, while conversion was used descriptively. XGBoost and LightGBM achieved validation AUC-ROC values of 0.94467 and 0.94455, respectively. The Spearman rank correlation between XGBoost predicted visit probabilities and Causal Forest estimated treatment effects was 0.3942 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.3873–0.4020), indicating a moderate association between predictive response and estimated incremental treatment benefit. At a 30% intervention budget, full-test-set policy values were 0.047333 for XGBoost and 0.046827 for Causal Forest, with corresponding net benefits of 0.045833 and 0.045327. In a separate 20,000-observation treatment-stratified evaluation subset, paired-bootstrap comparisons produced a Causal Forest–XGBoost policy-value difference of 0.001200 (95% CI: −0.000903 to 0.003600) and a net-benefit difference of 0.001177 (95% CI: −0.000945 to 0.003562). Neither difference was statistically distinguishable from zero. These findings demonstrate that predictive discrimination, treatment-effect ranking, and intervention utility represent distinct evaluation objectives. The results provide empirical evidence of their complementary roles within the Criteo benchmark but do not establish universal causal-policy superiority or cross-domain generalizability.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

Chemical safety is at a crossroads. Traditional animal-based regulatory testing is increasingly challenged for its limited human relevance, high costs, ethical concerns, and inability to cope with the scale of chemical innovation. Two complementary concepts have emerged from opposite ends of the safety spectrum: Green Toxicology (GT), which integrates toxicological considerations early into chemical design to “design-out” hazards, and the Human Exposome (HE), which aims to map the totality of real-world exposures across the human life span and links them to disease burden. While developed independently, GT and HE converge on a shared technological backbone of new approach methodologies (NAMs), microphysiological systems (MPS), exposomics, artificial intelligence, and probabilistic risk assessment. GT provides the upstream leverage point of prevention, while HE offers the downstream diagnostic power of surveillance. Their fusion is proposed to create a dynamic design–monitor–redesign innovation loop, in which each candidate is evaluated prospectively during design and then monitored and re-evaluated in real-world use through exposure surveillance. This framework could strengthen regulatory confidence, support substitution without regrettable outcomes, and align with international initiatives such as REACH, TSCA reform, and OECD test guideline modernization. Beyond science and regulation, the integration could yield economic and societal dividends: potential economic benefits from shared research infrastructure, accelerated replacement of animal testing, and the advancement of environmental justice by linking safer design to exposure equity. Together, GT and HE can establish the foundation for a 21st century chemical safety paradigm that is scientifically modern, economically compelling, innovation-driving, ethically aligned, and socially just.

Large digitised media collections often remain unprocessed and unexplored, despite being technically preserved, and archival institutions increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI). Rather than pursuing autonomous archival systems, this article examines how AI can support archival description and classification while preserving the contextual, historical and provenance-related integrity of archival materials. Drawing on the archive of media artist Teoman Madra (1931–2025), the study develops and evaluates an AI-assisted archival tool for a large, initially unstructured collection. The proposed approach establishes an iterative, human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI-generated suggestions are critically assessed by the archivist, whose decisions subsequently inform the system's outputs. The study shows that the controlled vocabulary given to the model shapes what it can recognise, that the archivist's validated decisions guide classification reliably within an archival unit but not across units, and that the model's contribution declines as tasks demand contextual knowledge beyond what is visible. While this process can improve efficiency and reveal details a person might miss, it also introduces epistemic risks, particularly when plausible but inaccurate classifications remain undetected. Faster processing does not by itself mean more reliable description. The article conceptualises AI-assisted archival classification as archival affirmation, a collaborative process in which human judgement remains integral to the production and validation of archival knowledge. By situating the archivist's interpretive authority at the centre of this process, the article contributes to discussions of the responsible integration, critical oversight and governance of AI in archival practice.

Eliyas Kebede Zemedkun, in his treatise From the Age of Reason to the Age of Algorithm, critically examines human sociocultural and political evolution, tracing the shift from mythological bewilderment and the worship of Logos to empiricism and the ultimate apotheosis of the algorithm. The author shows how truth migrated from God and mind to machines, leaving humanity excluded from knowledge production to become mere receivers. This technological deity operates as both servant and master, subsuming divine and demonic traits under automated architectures.Addressing the post human predicament, Zemedkun argues that surrendering truth, justice, and religion to algorithms evacuates human agency. Surveillance capitalism shifts from physical labor exploitation to cognitive exploitation, harvesting human thoughts, language, and art to train artificial intelligence models. Through the automation paradox, artificial intelligence accelerates capitalist self destruction by displacing industrial labor and eviscerating public purchasing capacity. Applying Nietzschean philosophy and the master slave dialectic, the author warns that delegating thought kills the will to power, creating the Last Man and reducing future generations to prompting animals. Foucault disciplinary power, Marcuse one dimensional digital man, and Derrida textual deconstruction trap humanity in simulated reason, shifting the paradigm from I think therefore I am to I prompt therefore I am.To rescue the general will from digital anarchy, Zemedkun introduces the Information Contract as a reciprocal normative commitment among citizens and institutions to protect information integrity based on mutual veracity. Distinguishing state formation as hardware from nation building as software, the author emphasizes that sustainable nations require information integrity rather than foundations built on myths. Concluding that the cognitive will to truth is what has died, Zemedkun asserts that society must embrace the Information Contract to avoid collapsing into a digital Hobbesian state of nature.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is commonly used to generate answers, assist writing, and provide feedback. In this role, educators use GenAI to surface assumptions and identify alternative interpretations when planning, designing, or making decisions across cultural and educational contexts. Drawing on work in global competence, intercultural competence, global citizenship education, and GenAI-supported critical feedback, this article presents a guided inquiry process for educators. The process begins with a real question, uses GenAI to surface possibilities, examines those possibilities through relevant evidence and input from people with experience in the setting, and then returns to the original decision. The aim is to expand professional inquiry while keeping interpretation and judgment with the educator.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.

documents.abstract: Predictive maintenance is a crucial approach in the industrial sector, and the utilization of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensors is becoming popular to detect faults and monitor the equipment’s condition. Still, the gathering, processing, and transmission of a large volume of data in predictive maintenance is highly challenging. To tackle such issues, this paper develops the Recurrent Radial Basis Long Short-Term Memory (RRBLSTM)-based predictive maintenance system using IIoT. The IIoT simulation is the primary process for a predictive maintenance system. The input time series data is subjected to the Box-Cox transformation for data transformation. The interval features, Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), and Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) features are extracted. The RRBLSTM is developed to label the issue. Using the predictive labels, the prompt is generated. The prompt is converted into a sentence by the utilization of the Generative Pre-trained Transformer NEOX Large Language Model (GPT-NEOX LLM) model. In addition, metrics like Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), R-Square, Mean Square Error (MSE), and Root MSE (RMSE) are used to estimate the efficacy of the model, and the corresponding outcome of 0.325, 0.901, 0.098, and 0.313.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND High rates of psychological distress among university students, together with persistently low use of professional mental health services, have become a notable public health issue. AIM To examine how help-seeking attitudes, stigma and individual psychological characteristics jointly shape university students’ preferences for different counseling formats. METHODS A cross-sectional survey was conducted which included 313 university students. Latent profile analysis was applied to identify distinct subgroups based on help-seeking attitudes and perceived stigma. Differences in psychological symptoms and preferences for artificial intelligence (AI) counseling were then compared across these subgroups. RESULTS The following three subgroups were identified: “Low willingness-high stigma” (36.4%), “moderate willingness-moderate stigma” (43.8%), and “high willingness-low stigma” (19.8%). Interestingly, the “low willingness-high stigma” group showed the most severe depression and anxiety symptoms, and reported the highest prior use of AI-based support and the strongest preference for AI counseling. CONCLUSION AI and human counselors play complementary roles: AI offers advantages in accessibility and anonymity, while human counselors remain irreplaceable in terms of empathy, complex problem-solving, and long-term therapeutic relationships.

Choosing an AI model for business is not simply about picking the most popular platform or the model with the strongest benchmark score. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini can all support business teams, but they differ in how they handle reasoning, writing, multimodal tasks, integrations, and ecosystem compatibility. The best AI model for business is the one that fits your actual workflows, data requirements, and long-term AI strategy. What makes an AI model suitable for business? Different teams expect different things from AI. Some companies may need strong writing and analysis capabilities, while others may prioritize multimodal workflows, automation, internal knowledge support, or integration with existing tools. That is why an AI model comparison for business should focus on practical use cases rather than model popularity alone. Teams need to understand how each option performs in the environments where it will actually be used. Comparing Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are all capable AI platforms, but they are not interchangeable. Their strengths may differ depending on the type of work being performed and the ecosystem in which the company operates. For example, one model may be a better fit for long-form reasoning or content generation, while another may be stronger for multimodal tasks, integrations, or workflows connected to a particular technology stack. A useful comparison should therefore look at capabilities in the context of real business tasks. Choosing the right AI model Choosing the right AI model starts with understanding the problem you want AI to solve. Instead of adopting a platform because competitors are using it, businesses should identify the workflows where AI can provide measurable value. This may include internal knowledge support, content creation, research, data analysis, automation, or customer-facing tools. Once the use case is clear, teams can compare model capabilities, costs, integration options, and operational requirements more effectively. Enterprise considerations For larger organizations, the decision becomes more complex. An enterprise AI model comparison should consider not only performance, but also security, compliance, governance, scalability, integration requirements, and user adoption. The model may eventually become part of daily operations across several departments, which means long-term maintainability and compatibility with internal systems matter just as much as individual features. Final thoughts There is no single best AI model for business that works for every company. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini each offer different strengths, and the right choice depends on how AI will be used inside the organization. By focusing on real workflows, integration requirements, security expectations, scalability, and business goals, companies can make a more practical AI model comparison for business and choose a platform that supports both current needs and future AI adoption.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can already participate in literature retrieval, question generation, coding, analysis, interpretation, and manuscript production, making fixed task-based rules about what should remain human increasingly unstable. This conceptual article introduces a Counterfactual Boundary Test for distinguishing why human involvement is retained in AI-assisted research. The test asks whether the rationale for human involvement would disappear if the relevant AI limitation disappeared. If so, the ground is capability-contingent; if the rationale persists because the work continues to be substantively attributed to human authors, the ground is human-authorship-related; other ethical, legal, fiduciary, political, or social grounds may remain distinct. Current hallucination and verification risks illustrate the first case, whereas comprehension, critical evaluation, justified acceptance, and accountability provide a parsimonious diagnostic synthesis for examining the second. The framework does not claim that all future science must remain human. Instead, it clarifies which rationales may move with technological capability and which arise specifically under human-authored science. These indicators do not replace the cumulative International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) authorship criteria. A worked citation-validation example illustrates selective revision of controls, and a specialist-coauthor case explains justified reliance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can expand the resources available for primary mathematics teaching, but assisted task completion is not the same as mathematical learning. This article develops a Human-Centred AI Pedagogy Framework through a synthesis of sociocultural theory and humans-with-media, human-centred AI and hybrid intelligence, social cognitive theory, TPACK and its AI extensions, and Ubuntu-informed relational ethics. The framework connects pedagogical intentionality, teacher agency, learner agency, mathematical sense-making, and ethical and relational responsibility. Its proposed explanatory contribution concerns the destination of mathematical decisions in a teacher–child–AI relationship. When teachers reduce direct guidance, decisions may be delegated to children or taken over by the system; this paper describes the latter possibility as decision drift. Agency handover, therefore, means increasing children's supported responsibility for strategy, representation, justification, and help-seeking, while teachers retain safeguarding and instructional accountability. The dimensions are differentiated as prerequisites, enabling conditions, mediating processes, outcomes and ethical boundaries. Two hypothetical lessons, on Grade 3 place value and Grade 5 growing patterns, illustrate the framework and compare AI-supported and non-AI alternatives. South African multilingualism, unequal infrastructure and teacher workload specify important implementation conditions. Five propositions identify expected relationships, observable indicators and competing explanations, providing a basis for classroom observation and comparative studies. Evidence from older learners motivates the analysis but does not establish effects in primary classrooms. The framework's explanatory and predictive validity remains to be tested; its value is a more precise account of what AI-mediated mathematical activity should enable, protect and make open to investigation.

documents.abstract: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load ( t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation ( t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cybersecurity systems to support threat detection, security monitoring, incident analysis, and decision-making. The ability of AI systems to process large volumes of security information and provide rapid recommendations can improve the efficiency of cybersecurity operations. However, the increasing dependence on AI may also influence how humans evaluate security information and respond to potential threats. In particular, differences in AI reliability may affect user trust, confidence, independent verification, and vigilance during cybersecurity decision-making. This paper examines the relationship between AI reliability and human vigilance in AI-assisted cybersecurity decision loops, with particular attention to trust, decision accuracy, confidence, verification behaviour, and human judgement. Drawing on existing literature related to human-AI collaboration, automation bias, cybersecurity decision-making, trust in AI, and cognitive behaviour, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI reliability, human trust, cognitive vigilance, verification behaviour, and cybersecurity decision quality. The paper considers AI as a decision-support mechanism rather than a complete replacement for human judgement. While reliable AI recommendations may support faster and more effective decisions, inappropriate reliance on AI may reduce independent evaluation and increase the possibility of accepting incorrect recommendations. The proposed framework provides a basis for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI reliability influence human vigilance and decision-making in cybersecurity environments.

Humans consistently outperform state-of-the-art AI models in action recognition, particularly in challenging real-world conditions involving low resolution, occlusion, and visual clutter.e those utilised by humans Understanding the sources of this performance gap is essential for developing more robust and human-aligned models. In this paper, we present a large-scale human AI comparative study of egocentric action recognition using human-defined Minimal Identifiable Recognition Crops (MIRCs), defined as the smallest spatial or spatiotemporal regions sufficient for reliable human recognition. We used our previously introduced, Epic-ReduAct, a systematically spatially reduced and temporally scrambled dataset derived from 36 EPIC-KITCHENS videos, spanning multiple spatial reduction levels and temporal conditions. Recognition performance is evaluated using over 3,000 human participants, Side4Video, and Qwen 3.5 9B models. Our analysis combines quantitative metrics, Average Reduction Rate and Recognition Gap, with qualitative analyses of spatial (high-, mid-, and low-level visual features) and spatiotemporal factors, including a categorisation of actions into Low Temporal Actions (LTA) and High Temporal Actions (HTA). Results show that human performance exhibits sharp declines when transitioning from MIRCs to sub-MIRCs, reflecting a strong reliance on sparse, semantically critical cues such as hand object interactions. In contrast, the model degrades more gradually and often relies on contextual and mid- to low-level features, sometimes even exhibiting increased confidence under spatial reduction. Temporally, humans remain robust to scrambling when key spatial cues are preserved, whereas the model often shows insensitivity to temporal disruption, revealing class-dependent temporal sensitivities. Overall, our findings demonstrate that strong benchmark performance can obscure fundamental human AI misalignment and highlight limitations in current spatial and spatiotemporal representations, suggesting concrete directions for more efficient and human-aligned action recognition systems.

documents.abstract: Quick developments in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have ushered in an era where highly realistic manipulated videos are now being produced at an unprecedented pace, which has thrown a big challenge to the authenticity of digital media, cybersecurity, public trust, and information integrity online. Most of the prior works on deepfake detection have been dedicated to either spatial feature extraction or temporal sequence modeling, and fall short in addressing the increasingly powerful deep learning-based deepfake samples. To overcome such drawbacks, this paper introduces an Attention-Enhanced Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Robust Deepfake Video Detection and Analysis, which combines EfficientNetB2 to extract discriminative spatial features and a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (Bi-GRU) with the inclusion of an Attention Mechanism to learn temporal features adaptively. The proposed framework is able to effectively account for visual artifacts at a frame level and long-range temporal inconsistencies within manipulated videos. In addition, three universal architectures, namely Hybrid Transformer, Temporal Pooling, and CNN3D, are used as baseline models for comparison. Here, experiments are performed on a balanced set of 2,952 authentic and manipulated videos, using a uniform frame sampling, a uniform image normalization, and a uniform preprocessing. Class-weighted loss with the AdamW optimizer is used to train the models and evaluate the models with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC). The results of the experiments presented in this paper demonstrate that the proposed Hybrid_GRU_Attention model can attain the highest detection performance with high accuracy of 95.75% and high AUC of 0.9771, which are better than the existing baseline models with high computational efficiency. The suggested solution gives a trustworthy and scalable choice in multimedia forensics, digital content validation, and future deepfake detection applications.

Twice the Septuagint speaks the name Ἀνατολή, and both times it speaks it to Ἰησοῦς the high priest (Zech 3:8; 6:11–12). Philo takes the name for the Logos and withholds the name of the one it was spoken to (4.4). The cut leaves a socket: the place of a name that a reader of the Septuagint supplies (4.4a). The Apocalypse sets a figure robed as Zechariah's Ἰησοῦς in the midst of the lampstands and names him (7a.9), and gives the one who conquers a name "ὃ οὐδεὶς οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ λαμβάνων" (2:17; 7b.10). What the sources distribute, the Apocalypse concentrates: names, offices, a garment, a judgment and a voice, spread across Zechariah, Philo's treatises and the Septuagint, are gathered on one named figure. Hebrews makes the same gathering in seven verses, the son of Nun, the dividing Logos and the great high priest named Ἰησοῦς (Heb 4:8–14; 7a.8). The rapid expansion of the Fourth Industrial Revolution presents a significant risk of widening the gendered digital skills gap in Sub-Saharan Africa, where women and youth face structural barriers to technological access. This paper evaluates an alternative, inclusive approach to digital transformation through an empirical case study of YAKILI's offline-first educational ecosystem in Cameroon, executed in coordination with the Secretariat of Education (SEDUC). Bridging the infrastructure deficit with an offlinefirst deployment architecture, the platform integrates a bilingual animated curriculum with a localized artificial intelligence assistant—the "YAKILI TEACHER BUDDY"—to foster professional agency and digital fluency. This mixed-methods case study analyzes a 10-month pilot encompassing 10 private school institutions, 40 digitalized classrooms, 590 up-skilled educators, and 7,800 active learners. Crucially, the data is disaggregated by gender to track the specific integration of female leadership and youth demographics. The findings demonstrate a 99.8% system runtime availability rate, a significant reduction in lesson planning fatigue, and an increase in self-reported technical efficacy among female teachers. The study concludes by discussing inherent sample limitations and outlining future longitudinal research vectors.

Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming pedagogical practices in Cameroonian secondary education. This study assesses the influence of teachers' experience using GenAI tools on how secondary school teachers in Yaoundé perceive the reliability and compliance of generated content with the guidelines of the Competency-Based Approach (CBA). Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, 370 teachers were surveyed by questionnaire and 130 others through semi-structured interviews (total N = 500). The Chi-square test reveals a highly significant association between GenAI user status and the perception of the quality of generated content (χ 2 (3) = 41.527; p < 0.001; Cramer's V = 0.335). Among users, 33.46% described the content as "contextual" compared to 15.38% of non-users. The interviews explain this difference through the progressive learning of contextual prompt engineering. However, 65.9% of all respondents judged the generated lesson plans to be poorly compliant with CBA guidelines. The study concludes that while direct experience improves the perception of GenAI, the structural deficit in African contextualization of large language models remains a major obstacle, which only targeted prompt engineering training and the development of better-adapted tools will be able to overcome.

documents.abstract: Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

This review systematically identifies and synthesizes implementation barriers reported in the literature regarding artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support systems in oncology. Following PRISMA guidelines, an initial search of the Scopus and PubMed databases and a subsequent citation-prioritized update identified review articles published between January 2021 and December 2025, of which 113 met the inclusion criteria. The review addresses five interconnected barriers: model interpretability, external validation, fairness and class imbalance, electronic health record integration, and data standardization. External validation is the most frequently cited challenge (73.5%), followed by model interpretability (66.4%) and data standardization (65.5%). Temporal trends show a marked increase in validation concerns, from 56.7% in 2021 to 93.8% in 2025, and declining attention to fairness barriers, from 53.3% in 2021 to 37.5% in 2025. This paper makes four main contributions. First, it presents an integrative framework showing that the barriers form an interconnected system in which fairness propagates into all downstream components, so that the observed decline in explicit fairness research signals a critical gap in current priorities. Second, it quantifies barrier prevalence and its temporal evolution, enabling evidence-based prioritization. Third, it consolidates the approaches reported in the literature into unified pipelines for bias mitigation and model interpretation. Fourth, it proposes a stage-specific implementation protocol with a decision flowchart to guide barrier assessment before deployment in screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis applications. The findings indicate that effective AI implementation in oncology requires addressing multiple barriers simultaneously rather than in isolation. The proposed frameworks and implementation protocol provide actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners working to translate AI models from development to clinical practice.

Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as persistent contaminants within wastewater systems, where treatment processes redistribute particles between effluent and sludge, thereby creating multiple pathways for exposure across both aquatic and terrestrial environments. However, meaningful comparisons among studies remain difficult due to substantial methodological variability in sampling strategies, particle-size thresholds, matrix preparation procedures, analytical techniques, reporting metrics, and quality assurance practices. This critical narrative review synthesizes recent advances in particle-resolved and mass-based analytical methods, artificial intelligence (AI), risk assessment, One Health frameworks, and governance, with particular emphasis on implementation challenges in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The literature reviewed demonstrates that no single analytical technique is capable of comprehensively characterizing particle abundance, size, morphology, polymer composition, and mass across all relevant environmental matrices. Consequently, the integration of complementary analytical approaches may provide more robust characterization, although their applicability remains dependent on matrix-specific validation requirements and resource availability. AI-based tools show considerable potential for automating particle detection, spectral classification, and selected treatment-modeling applications. Nevertheless, their broader transferability is constrained by the limited availability of representative datasets and insufficient independent validation. Evidence relating to human health confirms internal exposure to MPs in the biological samples investigated and highlights several plausible toxicological mechanisms, as well as emerging epidemiological associations. Despite these findings, causal relationships between MP exposure and adverse health outcomes, together with environmentally relevant exposure-response relationships, remain uncertain. At the same time, governance challenges are compounded by deficiencies in analytical infrastructure, methodological standardization, financing mechanisms, and data availability. Drawing on this synthesis, we propose a tiered and networked framework that combines accessible screening approaches, sentinel-site polymer confirmation, shared regional analytical facilities, computational tools, and harmonized quality assurance measures to strengthen MP monitoring in LMIC wastewater systems. Importantly, this framework should be regarded as a context-specific implementation proposal rather than a validated or universally optimal model. Its technical feasibility, economic requirements, scalability, and regulatory value require further assessment. Ultimately, meaningful progress in addressing MP contamination will depend on coordinated advances in analytical capacity, scientific evidence generation, sustainable financing, and effective governance.

documents.abstract: AI is slowly changing how education is planned, delivered and assessed. With machine learning, natural language processing and learning analytics, a platform can respond better to the different needs of its students. This paper looks at what AI can do in education and sets out a conceptual framework for an intelligent learning environment, one that combines learner information, adaptive materials, automated feedback and guidance from teachers. It covers personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, regular assessment, early identification of learning difficulties and accessibility. It also takes up the concerns that come with these tools: student privacy, bias, unequal access to technology, inaccurate AI-generated content, academic honesty and overdependence. The paper rests on a focused review of selected academic and policy literature. It reports no new experiment and no original student data. Its argument is that AI can make learning more supportive and flexible when used responsibly, and that it should assist teachers and students rather than replace the judgement, effort and human contact that education depends on.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

documents.abstract: This paper examines four case studies of alternative educational technology initiatives resisting Big Tech's dominance in education. Situated in Catalonia, Valencia, Brazil, and Argentina, these initiatives develop responses grounded in open technologies, collective action, and commitments to digital sovereignty. Drawing on the analytical dimensions of critical consciousness, collective engagement, and the construction of alternative educational technologies, we examine how situated practices move beyond critique as an exclusively intellectual exercise. The cases are not proposed as scalable alternatives of big tech solutions, but aim at revealing how collective action can enact context-specific forms of resistance and infrastructural autonomy within hybrid socio-technical environments.The findings highlight the importance of heterogeneity and pragmatism in responding to datafication and platformisation. In doing so, the article argues for a reconceptualisation of critique as a methodological practice: one that not only diagnoses the infrastructures, power relations, and harms associated with platformisation, but also explores how alternative sociotechnical futures can be enacted through situated collective action.

Purpose In vitro gametogenesis (IVG) has the potential to transform assisted reproduction by generating functional gametes from pluripotent stem cells and expanding access to genetic parenthood. However, a less explored consequence is its potential to enable the production of hundreds of embryos, fundamentally changing the scale and nature of embryo selection. This paper examines how such “embryo abundance” could intensify existing ethical concerns surrounding preimplantation genetic testing, polygenic embryo screening, and artificial intelligence-driven embryo ranking. Methods This paper presents a conceptual and ethical analysis of the implications of large-scale embryo production and selection enabled by IVG, focusing on reproductive autonomy, disability, procreative beneficence, inequality, and the commercialisation of reproductive medicine. Results Increasing the number of embryos available for selection may shift reproductive decision-making from therapeutic medicine towards reproductive optimization, creating new pressures to select the perceived “best” embryo. As selection becomes increasingly technologically feasible and socially normalized, reproductive choice may paradoxically evolve into expectations of reproductive responsibility. Conclusions IVG requires anticipatory ethical and regulatory consideration extending beyond questions of safety and access. Governance must address not only whether IVG can be introduced safely, but also how large-scale embryo selection may reshape understandings of reproductive autonomy, human variation, and responsible parenthood.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pharmacy education faster than curricula have adapted, yet evidence on how pharmacy students in sub-Saharan Africa understand and use it is almost absent. We assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) regarding AI among pharmacy students in a Francophone (Guinea) and an Anglophone (Malawi) country, and identified their determinants. Methods A multicentre online cross-sectional survey (29 March–12 June 2026) included pharmacy students from three universities in Conakry, Guinea, and from Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Malawi. A bilingual self-administered questionnaire measured knowledge (9 items), attitudes (8 Likert items) and practices (7 items, score 0–11). Prespecified cut-offs defined adequate knowledge (≥ 70%), favourable attitude (≥ 75%) and adequate practice (≥ 8/11). Multivariable logistic regression models, structured along the KAP pathway, estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 participants (Guinea 115, Malawi 207; median age 23 years), 99.7% had heard of AI and 96.2% had used AI tools, but only 27.9% had received formal AI training. Adequate knowledge was found in 32.0% (95% CI 27.1–37.3), favourable attitudes in 30.2% (25.4–35.4) and adequate practices in 64.3% (58.9–69.3). Half of the students (49.8%) believed that AI always provides correct results, and only 18.9% always verified AI-generated information. The two countries showed mirror-image profiles: Malawian students knew AI applications better and were more favourable to AI (aOR 3.77; 1.79–7.97), whereas Guinean students more often recognised AI's limitations and verified its outputs. Adequate practice was independently associated with adequate knowledge (aOR 2.28; 1.26–4.13) and favourable attitude (aOR 2.57; 1.40–4.73), and inversely with age > 23 years (aOR 0.39; 0.21–0.74) and studying in Malawi (aOR 0.39; 0.19–0.81). Advanced years of study predicted adequate knowledge (≥ 5th year: aOR 4.62; 1.27–16.87), while self-reported formal AI training was not associated with better knowledge. Conclusions Pharmacy students in both countries use AI almost universally but lack the critical knowledge needed to use it safely, with a high risk of automation bias. Curricula should move beyond tool familiarity towards structured, competency-based AI literacy centred on output verification, limitations, ethics and pharmacist accountability, adapted to each national context.
