documents.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), has been widely discussed in second language writing research as a promising form of support, earlier studies have not compared the quality of the same writers’ work when they compose with and without it. Furthermore, it remains uncertain whether GenAI consistently enhances writing quality across individuals. The present study employs both quantitative and qualitative approaches to assess whether GenAI improves the analytic quality of individual second language writers’ essays and to explore whether, and if so, why certain writers’ experience declines in particular components of writing quality. All participants completed two essays in a fixed sequence, first without GenAI assistance and then with it, which may constitute a potential limitation of the study design. The quantitative analyses indicated that, overall, essays written with GenAI assistance received higher scores across all four analytic components (task response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy) than essays written without GenAI assistance. Yet this pattern was not consistent; some writers actually declined on specific components. The qualitative analyses then identified three themes that explain lower scores in particular domains when GenAI was used: (1) the prioritization of content and evidence during GenAI interaction over the management of the overall demands of the task, which led to inadequate task fulfillment and formatting; (2) the inclusion of GenAI suggestions without sufficient attention to integration or coherence; and (3) a relative lack of attention to vocabulary and grammar revision. These results point to the importance of instructional interventions that support effective GenAI use and AI literacy among second language writers, and suggest that GenAI-based systems should be customized to align with writers’ specific needs and the specific components of task requirements.

The present text analyses the impact of artificial intelligence in sport from a dogmatic criminal law perspective, focusing on its effects on the configuration of risk, objective imputation, and duties of care. Starting from the premise that AI cannot be a subject of criminal liability, it is argued that its use reconfigures contexts of human action and requires a reinterpretation of classical categories such as permitted risk, professional negligence, and corporate criminal liability. The study examines scenarios of sports injuries mediated by algorithmic systems, emphasizing the central role of effective human control and risk organization. It also incorporates an analysis of good governance and technological compliance as preventive criminal-law prerequisites, as well as a reference to electronic sports, concluding that criminal liability remains human and organizational in nature, albeit mediated by technology.

documents.abstract: Background Large language model (LLM)–powered virtual patient systems are gaining popularity in nursing education but also face persistent challenges, such as hallucinations and role inconsistency. Objective This paper reports the model architecture design, technical considerations, implementation challenges, and evaluation of an LLM-powered AI-assisted simulated-patient system integrated into a nursing triage simulation game. Methods The system integrated a Unity-based game client, with GPT-4o hosted through Microsoft AI Foundry to support real-time simulated-patient dialogue in Traditional Chinese using Cantonese syntax. This developmental study comprised exploratory model selection, formative student feedback–informed enhancement from Version 1 to Version 2, development-stage script-fidelity evaluation, and evaluation of system usability and the Net Promoter Score in 2 tutorial cohorts of nursing students. Results Key technical contributions include a layered hallucination mitigation architecture that combines grounded prompt inclusion, few-shot conversational exemplars, negative role constraints, and calibrated model parameters. In the predefined script-fidelity evaluation, script-inconsistent responses occurred in 78 of 125 (62.4%) Version 1 outputs and 21 of 125 (16.8%) Version 2 outputs—an absolute difference of 45.6 percentage points. The implementation process also addresses stateless API memory management, cloud-based safety filter calibration for domain-specific clinical prompts, and prompt engineering strategies to prevent role drift and hidden scenario information leakage. GPT-4o was selected as the production model through exploratory development testing that considered script consistency, Cantonese-language suitability, response latency, technical reliability, deployment feasibility, cost considerations, and Unity integration compatibility; 45 of 50 (90%) assessed GPT-4o responses were rated fully script-consistent. Conclusions This study demonstrates the development and real-world tutorial deployment of a Cantonese-language, LLM-powered simulated-patient system for nursing triage education. Integrating formative student feedback with structured technical debugging enabled iterative refinement of dialogue fidelity, role consistency, protected-information handling, and game interaction functions. The resulting Version 2 system provides a practical, contextually tailored approach to supporting scalable simulated-patient dialogue in nursing education.
